source_regions.literal_source_text: D.1 Hilbert space and Markov operator conventions Definition D.1 (Hilbert space notation) . Let \zeta be a probability measure. The real Hilbert space L^{2}(\zeta) consists of equivalence classes of measurable functions f such that \int f^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\zeta<\infty . Its inner product and norm are \langle f,g\rangle_{L^{2}(\zeta)}\coloneqq\int fg\,\mathrm{d}\zeta\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\|f\|_{L^{2}(\zeta)}\coloneqq\langle f,f\rangle_{L^{2}(\zeta)}^{1/2}\,. (D.1) We write L_{0}^{2}(\zeta)\coloneqq\Bigl\{f\in L^{2}(\zeta):\int f\,\mathrm{d}\zeta=0\Bigr\}\,. (D.2) When \zeta=\pi_{\eta} , we abbreviate the inner product and norm by \langle f,g\rangle and \|f\| . Two functions equal \zeta -almost everywhere represent the same vector. A closed linear subspace \mathcal{M}\subseteq L^{2}(\zeta) has orthogonal complement \mathcal{M}^{\perp}\coloneqq\{g:\langle f,g\rangle=0\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{M}\} . Its orthogonal projection is the unique bounded operator \mathsf{P}_{\mathcal{M}} for which \mathsf{P}_{\mathcal{M}}f\in\mathcal{M} and f-\mathsf{P}_{\mathcal{M}}f\in\mathcal{M}^{\perp} . All operators in the convergence analysis are bounded linear operators on the indicated Hilbert spaces unless explicitly stated otherwise. The adjoint \mathsf{L}^{*} is characterized by \langle\mathsf{L}f,g\rangle=\langle f,\mathsf{L}^{*}g\rangle . An operator is self-adjoint if \mathsf{L}=\mathsf{L}^{*} , a contraction if \|\mathsf{L}f\|\leq\|f\| , and unitary if it is onto and preserves norms. A self-adjoint involution, meaning \mathsf{L}^{2}=I , is unitary. For self-adjoint operators \mathsf{L}_{1},\mathsf{L}_{2} , \mathsf{L}_{1}\preceq\mathsf{L}_{2}\hskip 10.00002pt\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 10.00002pt\langle f,(\mathsf{L}_{2}-\mathsf{L}_{1})f\rangle\geq 0\hskip 10.00002pt\text{for every }f (D.3) is the Loewner order. If \mathsf{L} is self-adjoint, the spectral theorem defines \psi(\mathsf{L}) for bounded Borel functions \psi ; in particular \mathbf{1}_{E}(\mathsf{L}) is the orthogonal projection onto the spectral set E , and a non-negative operator has a unique non-negative square root. Definition D.2 (Markov operators and density evolution) . Let \mathcal{K}(z,\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}) be a Markov kernel preserving \zeta . Its Markov operator on observables is (\mathsf{K}f)(z)\coloneqq\int f(z^{\prime})\,\mathcal{K}(z,\mathrm{d}z^{\prime})\,. (D.4) It is a contraction on L^{2}(\zeta) . Its adjoint \mathsf{K}^{*} governs density evolution: if a law has density h with respect to \zeta , then its density after one step is \mathsf{K}^{*}h . Constants are fixed by both operators. If P\ll\zeta has density h , then \chi^{2}(P\|\zeta)=\|h-1\|_{\zeta}^{2}\,. (D.5) Consequently, an operator norm bound for \mathsf{K} on L_{0}^{2}(\zeta) gives the same bound for its adjoint \mathsf{K}^{*} , and hence gives \chi^{2} contraction.

source_regions.literal_source_text: Our target distribution is the joint law \pi_{\eta} defined in ( 2.6 ), and we set \mathfrak{H}\coloneqq L^{2}(\pi_{\eta}) . Recall from ( 3.11 ) that the ideal Proximal BPS has transition kernel \mathcal{K}\bigl((x,y),\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}y^{\prime}\bigr)=\delta_{2x-y}(\mathrm{d}y^{\prime})\,\bigl[\rho\,\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y^{\prime}}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})+(1-\rho)\,\mathcal{H}_{y^{\prime}}(x,\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})\bigr]\,, where \mathcal{H}_{y^{\prime}} is the conditional half-turn kernel from Proposition 3.2 . Since the algorithm is a discrete-time chain, its evolution is described by the induced one-step Markov operator on observables, (\mathsf{K}f)(x,y)\coloneqq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}f(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\,\mathcal{K}\bigl((x,y),\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}y^{\prime}\bigr)\,. Thus \mathcal{K} acts on probability laws, whereas \mathsf{K} is its induced action on observables. The first term in brackets in \mathcal{K} is the conditional resampling branch. After the auxiliary coordinate is updated to y^{\prime} , this branch replaces the x -coordinate by an independent draw from \pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y^{\prime}} . The associated conditional expectation operator is (\mathsf{P}f)(x,y)\coloneqq\int f(x^{\prime},y)\,\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)\mid Y=y]\,. (B.1) In particular, \mathsf{P}f depends only on the coordinate y . The range and kernel of \mathsf{P} are \begin{split}\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}&\coloneqq\operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P})=\{f\in\mathfrak{H}:f(x,y)=g(y)\text{ for some }g\in L^{2}(\pi_{\eta}^{Y})\}\,,\\ \mathfrak{H}_{\perp}&\coloneqq\ker(\mathsf{P})=\operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P}^{\perp})=\{f\in\mathfrak{H}:\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)\mid Y]=0\}\,.\end{split} (B.2) Here \mathsf{P}^{\perp}\coloneqq I-\mathsf{P} , so \mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}\oplus\mathfrak{H}_{\perp} and f=\mathsf{P}f+\mathsf{P}^{\perp}f . In the common terminology of hypocoercivity [ 14 , 21 ] , \operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P}) is the macroscopic subspace and its orthogonal complement is the microscopic subspace. Thus functions in \mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}} depend only on the coordinate y , whereas functions in \mathfrak{H}_{\perp} have zero mean under \pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y} for \pi_{\eta}^{Y} -almost every y .

regions.literal_source_text: Our target distribution is the joint law \pi_{\eta} defined in ( 2.6 ), and we set \mathfrak{H}\coloneqq L^{2}(\pi_{\eta}) . Recall from ( 3.11 ) that the ideal Proximal BPS has transition kernel \mathcal{K}\bigl((x,y),\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}y^{\prime}\bigr)=\delta_{2x-y}(\mathrm{d}y^{\prime})\,\bigl[\rho\,\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y^{\prime}}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})+(1-\rho)\,\mathcal{H}_{y^{\prime}}(x,\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})\bigr]\,, where \mathcal{H}_{y^{\prime}} is the conditional half-turn kernel from Proposition 3.2 . Since the algorithm is a discrete-time chain, its evolution is described by the induced one-step Markov operator on observables, (\mathsf{K}f)(x,y)\coloneqq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}f(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\,\mathcal{K}\bigl((x,y),\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}y^{\prime}\bigr)\,. Thus \mathcal{K} acts on probability laws, whereas \mathsf{K} is its induced action on observables. The first term in brackets in \mathcal{K} is the conditional resampling branch. After the auxiliary coordinate is updated to y^{\prime} , this branch replaces the x -coordinate by an independent draw from \pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y^{\prime}} . The associated conditional expectation operator is (\mathsf{P}f)(x,y)\coloneqq\int f(x^{\prime},y)\,\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)\mid Y=y]\,. (B.1) In particular, \mathsf{P}f depends only on the coordinate y . The range and kernel of \mathsf{P} are \begin{split}\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}&\coloneqq\operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P})=\{f\in\mathfrak{H}:f(x,y)=g(y)\text{ for some }g\in L^{2}(\pi_{\eta}^{Y})\}\,,\\ \mathfrak{H}_{\perp}&\coloneqq\ker(\mathsf{P})=\operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P}^{\perp})=\{f\in\mathfrak{H}:\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)\mid Y]=0\}\,.\end{split} (B.2) Here \mathsf{P}^{\perp}\coloneqq I-\mathsf{P} , so \mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}\oplus\mathfrak{H}_{\perp} and f=\mathsf{P}f+\mathsf{P}^{\perp}f . In the common terminology of hypocoercivity [ 14 , 21 ] , \operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P}) is the macroscopic subspace and its orthogonal complement is the microscopic subspace. Thus functions in \mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}} depend only on the coordinate y , whereas functions in \mathfrak{H}_{\perp} have zero mean under \pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y} for \pi_{\eta}^{Y} -almost every y .

regions.literal_source_text: We first apply this block notation to the reflection map \mathsf{U} from ( 2.14 ). We use the same symbol for its pullback on observables: (\mathsf{U}f)(x,y)\coloneqq f(\mathsf{U}(x,y))=f(x,2x-y)\,. (B.4) This pullback is self-adjoint and unitary, and hence has block matrix \mathsf{U}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}&\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\\ \mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}&\mathsf{U}_{\perp\perp}\end{pmatrix}\,. Here \mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}=\mathsf{P}\mathsf{U}\mathsf{P} maps \mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}} to itself, whereas \mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}=\mathsf{P}^{\perp}\mathsf{U}\mathsf{P} maps \mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}} to \mathfrak{H}_{\perp} . Since \mathsf{U} is self-adjoint and unitary, \mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}} is a self-adjoint contraction on \mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}} . Writing \mathsf{U}^{2}=I in blocks gives \mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}=I-\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}^{2}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\mathsf{U}_{\perp\perp}=-\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\,. (B.5)
